30 Minute Walk Education
cues:
30-Minute Walk Test 
Purpose: 
 To assess cardiovascular fitness, gait efficiency, and endurance capacity in a low-impact, sustainable format.
This test gives you insight into how well your body handles steady-state movement over time, and serves as a baseline for future progress.

How to Perform: 
 
Set a Timer for 30 Minutes: 
 This is a continuous walking test—you’ll walk non-stop for 30 minutes at a brisk but sustainable pace.

Choose Your Route: 
 A flat, even surface like a track, trail, or treadmill is best.
If you're outside, choose a loop or path where you can walk uninterrupted.

Walk at a Challenging but Comfortable Pace: 
 The pace should be fast enough to elevate your heart rate and breathing, but not so intense that you have to stop or slow down.
A good rule of thumb: You should be able to talk but not sing during the test.

Track Your Distance: 
 Use a GPS watch, pedometer, fitness tracker, or treadmill display to track total distance walked in 30 minutes.

Record Data Immediately After: 
 
 
Total distance (in miles or kilometers) 
Perceived exertion (Rate your effort 1–10) 
Heart rate at finish (if available) 
Recovery heart rate 1 minute after stopping (optional but valuable) 
 
Why It Matters: 
 
Distance walked is a direct indicator of cardiovascular endurance.
Effort level and recovery rate reflect how efficiently your body handles aerobic work.

name: 3D Ankle Drive
cues:
Exercise: 3D Ankle Drive 
Purpose: 
 The 3D Ankle Drive is a multiplanar ankle mobility drill that targets dorsiflexion, inversion, eversion, tibial rotation, and foot/arch dynamics in a functional, upright position. It helps improve: 
 
Closed-chain ankle dorsiflexion 
Dynamic foot and ankle control 
Hip and knee translation over the foot 
Gait and squat mechanics 
Reduces joint stiffness and compensations from upstream or downstream limitations 
 
Target Areas: 
 
Ankle joint (talocrural and subtalar joints) 
Posterior chain (gastroc, soleus, Achilles) 
Midfoot and forefoot mobility 
Tibial rotation and foot pronation/supination mechanics 
Also integrates hip and core engagement 
 
Setup: 
 
Stand in a half-kneeling or split stance (lunge position), or with one foot forward and flat on the ground. 
Use a wall, stick, or dowel for balance or tactile cueing if needed. 
 
Movement Pattern (3 Planes):.

Sagittal Plane (Forward Drive): 
 
Shift your front knee directly forward over your toes, driving toward the 2nd or 3rd toe. 
Keep the heel flat on the ground. 
You’re loading closed-chain dorsiflexion here.

Frontal Plane (Medial & Lateral Drive): 
 
From the same starting position, drive your front knee medially and laterally across the foot: 
Medial Drive: Knee toward big toe or inside of the foot (biases pronation/inversion mobility). 
Lateral Drive: Knee toward pinky toe (biases supination/eversion mobility). 
Keep the heel grounded, allowing the arch to respond dynamically.

Transverse Plane (Rotational Drive): 
 
Rotate your torso and pelvis over the planted ankle: 
Internal Rotation Drive: Rotate toward the front leg side (biases tibial IR + pronation). 
External Rotation Drive: Rotate away from the front leg (biases tibial ER + supination). 
The knee will naturally follow, creating spiral loading through the foot and ankle complex. 
 
Reps & Dosage: 
 
Perform 5–8 reps per direction, per leg 
Slow and controlled, emphasizing heel contact and range quality 
Great as part of movement prep or mobility work 
 
Key Coaching Points: 
 
Keep the heel glued to the ground — if it lifts, dorsiflexion is being lost. 
Don’t force range — move into tissue tension, not pain. 
Allow the foot to pronate and supinate naturally as the knee and torso move — don’t try to hold a static arch. 
Control the pelvis — avoid collapsing into hip adduction or lumbar extension. 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Ankle dorsiflexion isn't just sagittal — it's tri-planar. 
Improves real-world mobility demands for walking, squatting, jumping, and cutting. 
Helps unstick ankle joints and retrain foot control dynamically — ideal for athletes, runners, and lifters. 
Great for clearing asymmetries and improving force transfer from the ground up. 
 
When to Use: 
 
Pre-squat or pre-run warm-up 
Daily mobility work for ankle stiffness 
Rehab after ankle sprains, Achilles issues, or plantar fascia overload 
As part of a foot/ankle reset for arch control and proprioception 
 
Progressions: 
 
Add light weight (KB or plate) to load the movement 
Use elevated front foot for deeper ankle angles 
Incorporate breath holds or isometric end-range pushes 
Pair with toe spacers or barefoot work for even better foot integration.

90/90 Hip External Rotation Kinetic Stretching
cues: Position yourself in a 90/90 base position with your chest facing the direction of your front knee.

Placing your hands on either side of the front leg, shift your chest forward/up while shifting your pelvis back/up to create an external rotation stretch on the capsule of the hip that is on the ground.
Take a breath in and create a full body contraction and create a contraction on the inside of the front leg as if you were attempting to lift it straight up off the floor.
Use this regressive tissue contraction to slowly pull your tall chest towards the floor and deeper into a stretch of external rotation.
Find the basement of your stretch, then change directions and begin pressing the bottom of the front leg into the floor.
This progressive tissue contraction will drive your chest back up and to the starting position.
The amount of reps, the time for each direction/rep, and the amount of tension you create will be variables dependent on your program.
You can progress the difficulty by putting less tension into the groun with your hands, lifting your hands off the ground, holding a weight, or putting your hands overhead.
Make sure to keep a tall chest throughout and do not lose tension in the target hip.

name: 90/90 Hip Internal Rotation Kinetic Stretching
cues: Position yourself in a 90/90 base position with either your hands on the floor to your sides or hands clasped together in front of the chest.
Take a breath in and create a full body contraction, then begin working to lift the back foot off of the ground.
Slowly begin to rotate the spine and pelvis in the direction of the back hip until you reach your end range, then laterally flex the torso in the direction of the back foot.

Once you have reached your end range of internal rotation, begin pressing the back foot/ankle into the floor, then change directions and use that tension to drive yourself back to the starting position.
The amount of reps, the time for each direction/rep, and the amount of tension you create will be variables dependent on your program.
You can progress the difficulty by putting less tension into the ground with your hands, lifting the hands off of the ground, holding a weight, or putting your hands overhead.

A Run Coaching
cues:
Purpose: 
The "A" Run is designed to reinforce proper sprint mechanics, focusing on: 
 
Hip flexion (knee drive) 
Ankle dorsiflexion 
Postural integrity 
Rhythm and turnover 
It mimics the swing phase of sprinting and develops leg stiffness, limb timing, and vertical force application. 
 
Target Areas: 
 
Hip flexors (for knee drive) 
Hamstrings (for foot recovery) 
Glutes and calves (for support and stiffness) 
Core and postural muscles (for alignment and control) 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat, open space (10–20 yards or meters) 
Athletic footwear or barefoot (depending on surface and context) 
 
Movement Pattern:.

Posture First: 
 
Upright torso, tall spine 
Eyes forward, shoulders relaxed 
Core gently braced, ribs stacked over pelvis 
Arms bent at ~90°, moving front-to-back (not across body).

Cycle the Legs: 
 
Begin a rhythmic, alternating high-knee action, but focus on: 
Driving the knee up to roughly hip height 
Keeping the toe dorsiflexed (toes pulled up toward shin) 
Recovering the foot under the hip with each step.

Landing Mechanics: 
 
Land on the ball of the foot, directly under the center of mass 
Quick ground contact — think "punch and pull" 
Avoid excessive heel striking or bouncing vertically.

Progression and Flow: 
 
Keep the rhythm fast but controlled 
Start in place or moving slowly forward 
Progress to faster reps or resisted versions as skill improves 
 
Reps & Dosage: 
 
3–5 sets of 10–15 meters (in-place or moving) 
Rest as needed between sets to maintain crisp technique 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Drive the knee up, recover fast under the hip.” 
“Stay tall, strike quick.” 
“Toes up, foot under.” 
“Quiet feet, sharp arms.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Excessive vertical bounce (too much airtime, not enough force into the ground) 
Heel behind the body (overextending or pawing back too far) 
Low knee drive (cutting short the hip flexion) 
Lack of rhythm (arms and legs out of sync) 
Toes pointing down (poor dorsiflexion) 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Reinforces efficient leg mechanics for sprinting and acceleration 
Builds coordination and neuromuscular rhythm 
Improves leg retraction and ground prep — essential for reducing ground contact time 
Trains postural control and core stiffness during dynamic movement 
 
When to Use: 
 
As part of a sprint warm-up or sprint technique session 
In speed development drills for athletes 
As a movement re-integration tool during rehab from hamstring or hip flexor injuries 
Within plyometric or high-speed prep work.

name: A Skip Coaching
cues:
Exercise: A-Skip 
(aka: High Knee Skip, Frontside Sprint Mechanics Drill) 
Purpose: 
The A-Skip teaches and reinforces key elements of sprinting, especially the frontside cycle, including: 
 
Hip flexion and knee drive 
Ankle dorsiflexion (toe-up position) 
Ground contact under the hips 
Postural alignment and arm-leg coordination 
 
This is a foundational drill in any sprint prep routine, movement re-education, or return-to-run progression.

Target Areas: 
 
Hip flexors (knee lift mechanics) 
Ankle dorsiflexors (toe-up position) 
Glutes and hamstrings (stance leg support and timing) 
Core/trunk (postural control) 
Shoulder girdle (reciprocal arm swing) 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat surface (10–20 meters) 
Athletic shoes or barefoot on turf/track 
Performed after A-Walk and A-March 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Posture First: 
 
 
Stand tall, ribs stacked over pelvis 
Arms bent ~90°, ready to move opposite the legs 
 
 
Lift and Skip: 
 
 
Begin a skipping rhythm, where one leg drives the knee up to ~hip height 
Toe stays dorsiflexed (pointed up), with shin vertical or slightly forward 
The other leg pops off the ground quickly, supporting bodyweight through a quick, elastic contact 
 
 
Ground Contact: 
 
 
Land on the ball of the foot, directly under the center of mass 
The goal is quick, springy contact — not vertical height 
 
 
Rhythm and Arms: 
 
 
Arms swing naturally in sync with legs — avoid crossing midline 
Think about a bounce + drive + recover rhythm 
Perform continuously down the track or in place to build pattern 
 
Reps & Sets: 
 
2–3 sets of 10–20 meters 
Focus on technique and rhythm, not speed or power 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Knee up, toe up.” 
“Strike under the hip.” 
“Bounce and drive — snap it back.” 
“Stay tall, fast arms.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Overstriding — foot lands in front of body 
Dropping toe or lazy foot — lose dorsiflexion 
Collapsing posture — leaning back or forward excessively 
Arms crossing midline — losing rhythm 
Vertical bounding — focus is on rhythmic forward motion, not jumping high 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Rehearses sprint technique at low to moderate speed 
Builds neural coordination between upper and lower body 
Trains frontside mechanics — the most efficient and powerful part of sprinting 
Improves ground stiffness and quickness 
Supports rehab or gait retraining in a controlled, rhythmic way 
 
When to Use: 
 
Sprint warm-ups and speed sessions 
During return-to-run or running form development 
In plyometric progressions for force application timing 
For young or developing athletes learning sprint posture 
 
Progressions: 
 
A-Skip → A-Run 
Add resistance band around waist or sled for resisted skipping 
Add mini hurdles for rhythm and contact feedback 
Use tempo sets (e.g., 3 sets of 10m with increasing intensity).

name: A Walk Coaching
cues:
Exercise: "A" Walk 
(aka: Sprint Mechanics Walk, Knee Drive Walk) 
Purpose: 
The A-Walk teaches postural control, hip flexion, ankle dorsiflexion, and coordinated arm-leg rhythm in a low-speed environment.

It's a key drill for: 
 
Learning or reinforcing sprint mechanics 
Improving joint position awareness (hips, knees, ankles) 
Teaching frontside sprinting (knee drive, toe up, shin angle) 
Beginning return-to-sport or gait retraining 
 
Target Areas: 
 
Hip flexors (knee drive) 
Ankle dorsiflexors (toes up during swing phase) 
Glutes and hamstrings (stance control) 
Core and trunk stabilizers (postural alignment) 
Arm and shoulder rhythm (reciprocal swing) 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat space (10–15 yards) 
Shoes or barefoot depending on surface and training goal 
Focus is on deliberate movement, not speed 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Posture First: 
 
 
Stand tall, eyes forward, ribs stacked over pelvis 
Engage core and glutes gently 
Arms bent ~90°, ready to swing in opposition to legs 
 
 
Step and Drive: 
 
 
Step forward by lifting the knee to ~90°, with the toe dorsiflexed (pulled up toward shin) 
Strike the foot directly under the hip (not in front) 
As one leg drives up, the opposite arm swings forward naturally 
 
 
Controlled Rhythm: 
 
 
Move slowly and deliberately, emphasizing posture and mechanics 
Each step should feel like a miniature sprint cycle done in slow motion 
Keep the heel off the ground during stance — walk through the ball of the foot 
 
Reps & Dosage: 
 
2–3 sets of 10–15 yards 
Focus on quality over speed 
Can be repeated daily or as part of a sprint warm-up sequence 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Knee up, toe up.” 
“Strike under the hip.” 
“Posture tall, arms crisp.” 
“Drive, control, land quietly.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Overstriding — foot lands in front of body 
Toes pointing down — poor dorsiflexion 
Slouched posture — head forward, ribs flared 
Arms crossing midline — inefficient upper body motion 
Lack of rhythm — broken or robotic steps 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Builds a technical base for higher-speed sprint drills 
Reinforces frontside sprinting mechanics, which are more efficient and less injury-prone 
Great for developing athletes, or re-educating movement after injury 
Transfers to improved stride mechanics, acceleration, and posture 
 
When to Use: 
 
Start of sprint training warm-ups 
As part of a drill sequence (A-Walk → A-March → A-Skip → A-Run) 
During return-to-run or gait retraining protocols 
As a teaching tool in youth development or after layoff 
 
Progressions: 
 
A-March — increase speed and drive force 
A-Skip — add rhythm and ground reaction 
A-Run — faster cycle with bounce 
Add light resistance (banded walk) for motor patterning.

Ankle CAR How To
cues:
Purpose: 
Ankle CARs help you assess and improve active control of the full range of motion at the ankle joint (talocrural and subtalar).

The goal is to strengthen the joint capsule, improve motor control, and maintain healthy dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion, and eversion — all of which are critical for movement performance and injury prevention.

Target Areas: 
 
Ankle joint capsule 
Dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior) 
Plantarflexors (gastroc, soleus) 
Invertors / evertors (tibialis posterior, peroneals) 
Foot stabilizers 
 
Setup: 
You can perform Ankle CARs in seated, supine, or long seated (legs out in front) position.

Here's the most common and effective version: 
Position: Long Seated or Supine 
 
Sit or lie on your back with one leg extended.
Hug the working knee toward your chest so the shin is vertical and the ankle is free to move through space.
Hold under your thigh to prevent hip rotation or ankle compensation.
Keep toes relaxed unless intentionally extending/flexing.

Movement Pattern: Full Controlled Ankle Circle 
 
Start in Dorsiflexion 
 
 
Pull your foot up toward your shin.

Move into Inversion 
 
 
Without losing dorsiflexion, begin rotating the sole of your foot inward (toward midline).

Plantarflexion 
 
 
Continue the arc downward into plantarflexion (point your toes down), maintaining the circular path.

name: Ankle Circles
cues: Position the stick vertically in front of the body driving the base of the stick into the ground.
Perform ankle circles, putting the heel/toe raises and lateral ankle shifts together.
Shift back onto your heels and lift the toes.
Laterally shift to one side, rolling to the inside edge of one foot and outside edge of the other foot.
Shift forward onto your toes and lift the heels.
Laterally shift to the other side, rolling to the inside edge and outside edge of the feet in the opposite direction.
Complete 5-6 reps in each direction, always making sure to move under control.

name: Ankle Dorsiflexion from Combat Base
cues: Get into a combat base position with the working leg bent and foot flat on the floor.
Passive Stretch - achieve a passive stretch by shifting the body over the working leg while keeping the heel on the floor, closing down the angle of the ankle.
Work on breathing to relax and sink deeper into the stretch for 2+ minutes.

PAILs - take a breath in and create full body tension, then begin slowly pressing the bottom of the foot into the floor, building up the contraction to 100% over 10 seconds, then holding the max contraction for another 10 seconds.
RAILs - quickly switch directions, working to lift the bottom of the foot off of the floor, closing down the angle of the ankle at 100% effort for 15 seconds.
Relax into the new stretch position for 30 seconds up to 2 minutes and repeat for 1-2 more reps before switching sides.

cues: Begin lying on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Try to relax your low back, keeping it in a neutral position (which means you should feel a slight curve in your low back if you place the top of your hand under your back).
Turn "on" your core muscles and then flatten your low back against the floor by slightly tilting your pelvis upward.

name: Anti-Rotation Glute Bridge Series
cues: Lie on your back parallel to a wall with the arms straight up to the ceiling holding a stick with an overhand grip and driving the base of the stick into the wall.
The arms should be shoulder width with the elbows fully extended.
Start with the knees bent and feet and back flat to the floor.
Drive the stick laterally into the wall at about 40-60% tension.
Maintaining this tension, start by moving into bridges, tucking the tailbone and squeezing the glutes as you drive your hips up.
You can then make things more dynamic by performing a single-leg glute bridge while driving the other leg up into hip flexion.
Finally, move into an alternating march where you hold one hip in extension while the other hip drives up into flexion. Alternate between legs for reps while maintaining single-leg hip extension.
After completing the prescribed reps on the first side of the body, switch sides and repeat this process on the other side of the body.

name: B Run Coaching
cues:
Exercise: "B" Run 
(aka: B-Skip Run, Heel Recovery Drill, or Stride Cycle Drill) 
Purpose: 
The "B" Run trains the recovery and reapplication phase of the sprint cycle — mimicking what happens after toe-off when the leg cycles under the hip and prepares to strike the ground again. It emphasizes: 
 
Hamstring activation 
Knee extension timing 
Ground prep mechanics 
Leg stiffness and coordination 
 
It’s often used to teach efficient leg turnover, clean up overstriding, and reduce injury risk (especially to the hamstrings). 
Target Areas: 
 
Hamstrings (eccentric control during recovery) 
Hip flexors (for knee lift and leg cycling) 
Glutes and calves (for support and landing) 
Core and postural control 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat, open area (10–20 meters) 
Athletic footwear or barefoot on turf/track 
Warm up with A-March and A-Run before progressing to B variations 
 
Movement Pattern:.

Start with "A" Mechanics: 
 
Maintain an upright posture, tall spine 
Core braced, arms driving front-to-back rhythmically 
Start with knee drive and foot dorsiflexed — just like an A-skip or A-run.

Add the Extension Phase (the "B" part): 
 
After driving the knee up, extend the lower leg forward at the top of the cycle 
Then snap the leg back down into the ground by activating the hamstrings 
The foot should contact the ground under your center of mass, not far out in front 
Think of it like pawing or scraping the ground in a downward action — but done with control, not overemphasis.

Cycle Repetitively: 
 
Continue alternating legs, keeping the rhythm crisp 
Control the extension and retraction, especially at higher speeds 
 
Reps & Dosage: 
 
3–5 sets of 10–15 meters (walk back recovery) 
Focus on quality, not speed — this is a technical drill 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Lift, extend, snap down.” 
“Knee up, toe out, pull under.” 
“Strike under the hip, not in front.” 
“Quiet feet, controlled snap.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Overextending the leg — reaching too far forward with the foot 
Striking too far in front of the body — leads to braking and hamstring overload 
Too much bounce — losing horizontal force 
Not snapping down the leg — letting it drop passively 
Trunk collapse — maintain upright posture and arm rhythm 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Teaches the correct backside-to-frontside leg cycle 
Helps develop timing and control in the stride phase 
Strengthens the hamstrings eccentrically and dynamically 
Reduces risk of overstriding, hamstring strain, and loss of speed efficiency 
 
When to Use: 
 
In a sprint warm-up or technical session 
During return-to-sprint or hamstring rehab protocols 
As a drill to refine stride mechanics in speed development 
Before plyometric work or resisted sprint drills.

name: B Skip Coaching
cues:
Exercise: B-Skip 
(aka: Stride-Recovery Skip, Heel-Recovery Skip) 
Purpose: 
The B-Skip focuses on the leg’s recovery path during the sprint cycle — specifically: 
 
Driving the knee up 
Extending the lower leg (knee extension) 
Snapping the leg back down under the hip using the hamstrings 
 
It builds awareness and timing of the backside-to-frontside leg transition and reinforces a tight, efficient stride to reduce overstriding and improve sprint economy.

Target Areas: 
 
Hamstrings (eccentric control and retraction) 
Hip flexors (drive and lift) 
Glutes (postural control) 
Core (trunk stability during motion) 
Foot/ankle complex (contact stiffness and timing) 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat surface, 10–20 meters 
Performed after A-Skip in a sprint prep sequence 
Shoes or barefoot on turf or track 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Posture and Arm Mechanics: 
 
 
Stay tall with ribs stacked over hips 
Arms bent at ~90°, moving in opposition to the legs 
 
 
Skip Cycle: 
 
 
Begin with a knee drive (just like A-Skip) 
At the top of the knee drive, extend the leg forward (as if prepping for ground contact) 
Then, snap the leg down and under your center of mass, actively using the hamstring to pull the foot beneath you 
Land on the ball of the foot, directly under the hips — not out in front 
 
 
Cadence and Rhythm: 
 
 
The movement is bouncy and rhythmic, like a skipping cycle 
Focus on control and timing, not height or speed 
 
Reps & Sets: 
 
2–3 sets of 10–20 meters 
Performed slowly at first, then progressed to moderate intensity with crisp rhythm 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Knee up, extend out, snap down.” 
“Pull the foot back under your hips.” 
“Stay tall, land fast.” 
“Heel up and under, don’t fling behind.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Overextending the leg — reaching too far out front 
Not snapping the foot down — passive landing 
Heel flicking backward instead of cycling efficiently 
Lack of dorsiflexion — toes should be pulled up, not floppy 
Collapsing trunk or poor arm-leg coordination 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Teaches efficient recovery from the toe-off phase of the sprint 
Prevents overstriding and braking forces 
Strengthens the hamstrings eccentrically, reducing risk of injury 
Helps athletes feel and refine the transition phase of sprinting.

name: B Walk Coaching
cues:
Exercise: "B" Walk 
(aka: Heel Recovery Walk or Cycle Drill Walk) 
Purpose: 
The B-Walk builds on the A-Walk by introducing the leg recovery cycle — mimicking the transition from hip flexion to extension, while activating the hamstrings to “pull” the foot down under the body.

It develops: 
 
Hamstring control and eccentric awareness 
Knee extension timing 
Proper foot strike under the center of mass 
Improved stride mechanics and limb coordination 
 
Target Areas: 
 
Hamstrings (eccentric control during heel recovery) 
Hip flexors (driving the leg forward) 
Glutes and quads (postural support and stride alignment) 
Ankle dorsiflexors (maintain toe-up position) 
Core and upper body posture 
 
Setup: 
 
10–15 yards of flat space 
Light footwear or barefoot (on safe surface) to improve proprioception 
Ideal to follow A-Walk or A-March as a warm-up progression 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Start in Tall Posture: 
 
 
Stand upright with ribs stacked over pelvis 
Arms bent at ~90°, relaxed but ready to move in opposition to legs 
 
 
Step and Extend: 
 
 
Begin by driving the knee up like in A-Walk 
At the top of the stride, extend the lower leg forward 
Then pull the foot down and under your hip by activating the hamstring 
The foot should land directly beneath your center of mass, not in front 
 
 
Repeat with Control: 
 
 
Alternate sides with a deliberate tempo 
Move slowly enough to feel the cycle — up, extend, pull down 
 
Reps & Dosage: 
 
2–3 sets of 10–15 yards 
Done slowly and intentionally — this is coordination training, not conditioning 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Up, extend, snap down.” 
“Knee up, foot out, pull under.” 
“Land under the hip, not in front.” 
“Stay tall, soft and controlled.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Overstriding — foot landing too far in front 
Letting the foot drop passively instead of pulling down 
Excessive trunk lean or loss of posture 
Toe pointing down — ensure dorsiflexion is maintained 
Inconsistent arm swing — arms should move opposite the legs 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Reinforces backside-to-frontside transition in sprinting 
Builds awareness of hamstring involvement in stride recovery 
Teaches athletes to strike under their center of mass, improving sprint efficiency 
Acts as a precursor to B-Skip and B-Run, which develop reactivity and rhythm 
 
When to Use: 
 
As part of a sprint warm-up progression 
In gait retraining or return-to-run protocols 
For athletes needing improved stride control and efficiency 
In post-hamstring rehab for patterning before adding speed 
 
Progressions: 
 
B-Skip (adds rhythm and ground contact timing) 
B-Run (dynamic turnover with recovery pattern) 
Add mini hurdles for stride awareness 
Combine with wall drill knee drives and hip extension drills.

cues: Begin by kneeling on an exercise mat or floor, positioning your knees and feet hip-width apart, with your feet dorsiflexed toes pointing towards your body.
Slowly lean forward to place your hands on the mat, positioning them directly under your shoulders at shoulder-width with your fingers facing forward elbows extended.
Reposition your hands and knees as necessary so that your knees are directly under your hips and hands are directly under your shoulders.
Turn "on" your core and abdominal muscles to position your spine in a neutral position, avoid any excessive sagging or arching.
Slowly raise your knees a few inches from the floor and maintain a neutral spine.
Begin to squeeze shoulder blades down and back as if trying to touch them together chest moving toward the floor.
Elbows remain in extension.
Finally press shoulder blades away from spine with your chest moving away from the floor.
Repeat for prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Bear Shoulder Taps
cues: Begin by kneeling on an exercise mat or floor, positioning your knees and feet hip-width apart, with your feet dorsiflexed toes pointing towards your body.
Slowly lean forward to place your hands on the mat, positioning them directly under your shoulders at shoulder-width with your fingers facing forward.
Reposition your hands and knees as necessary so that your knees are directly under your hips and hands are directly under your shoulders.
Turn "on" your core and abdominal muscles to position your spine in a neutral position, avoid any excessive sagging or arching.
Slowly raise your knees a few inches from the floor and maintain a neutral spine.
Lift one hand from the floor and tap opposite shoulder.
Maintain neutral spine position while in three points of contact.
Lower hand back to starting positon.
Repeat for prescribed number of repetitions.

name: Bear Sit Hip Flexion Hover
cues: Position yourself in a bear sit base position with both sit bones on the floor and knees bent to 90 degrees.
Depending on your mobility, you may need to lean your torso forward or back to increase or decrease the challenge, but work to keep a tall chest throughout the set.
You can lean back with your arms extended behind you, clasp your hands together in front of your chest, or make fists with straight arms out to the sides.
Position an object to the outside of the working leg.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, and without moving any other part of the body, flex one hip and pull the knee as high into the air as you can.
Hover over the object, then slowly set it back on the floor on the other side.
Reset your body tension, flex the hip and bring it back over the object to the start position.
Complete for the designated number of reps.
Switch legs and repeat this process on the other side.
You can also set up multiple objects outside of the leg, causing you to complete multiple hover challenges with each rep.

name: Bear Sit Hip Flexion PRLO
cues: Position yourself in a bear sit base position with both sit bones on the floor and knees bent to 90 degrees.
Depending on your mobility, you may need to lean your torso forward or back to increase or decrease the challenge, but work to keep a tall chest throughout the set.
You can lean back with your arms extended behind you, clasp your hands together in front of your chest, or make fists with straight arms out to the sides.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, and without moving any other part of the body, flex one hip and pull the knee as high into the air as you can.
Hold for the designated period of time, then slowly set it back on the floor.
Reset your body tension, then complete for the designated number of reps.
Switch legs and repeat this process on the other side.

name: Bear Sit PRLO
cues: Position yourself in a bear sit base position with both sit bones on the floor and knees bent to 90 degrees, with your hands grasping your shins.
Depending on your mobility, you may need to lean your torso forward or back to increase or decrease the challenge.
No matter your torso position, work to keep a tall chest throughout the set.
Relax your body, then use your elbows to press your legs toward the floor, finding your passive end range of motion.
Then come out of the position 10-15 degrees so that you have space to actively contract into.
Take a breath in and create a full body contraction, and actively drive your legs toward the floor and away from the support of the arms.
Hold for the designated period of time, aiming to maintain an active contraction as close to your passive end range as possible.
After the time is up, relax your tension and bring your legs back to your arms.
Reset your tension and complete for the designated number of reps, holding a max contraction each time.

name: Bear Tricep Extension
cues: Begin by placing band in an anchored low position in the door.
Grab band with one hand facing the door in bear position (quadruped wrists in line and underneath shoulders, hip and knees in line, pelvis in neutral and core active).
Your body should be far enough from the anchor so that band would be tensioned with hand lifted off ground and elbow at your side next to waist.
With only 3 points of contact with the ground begin triceps extension (straightening elbow) with the hand holding band.
Keep shoulder depressed and retracted to avoid forward shoulder posture.
Repeat for prescribed number of sets and repetitions.
Repeat on opposite side.

name: Bent Leg Calf Stretch
cues: Using a club, stick, or any sturdy upright for balance, step one foot back and one foot forward.
Flex your back hip, knee, and ankle while keeping the heel on the floor.
Work to sit the hips back and drive the knee forward to increase the stretch on the lower side of the calf (soleus).
Focus on breathing to get the best stretch possible and hold for the prescribed amount of time before switching sides.

name: Big Toe Extension PAILs and RAILs
cues: Passive Stretch - achieve a passive stretch by placing the big toe on the edge of a wall, desk, or upright surface and hold the extension stretch for 2+ minutes.
PAILs - take a breath in and create full body tension, then contract the muscles being stretched by pressing the big toe into the wall, building up the contraction to 100% over the first 10 seconds.
Hold the max effort PAILs contraction for another 10 seconds.
RAILs - quickly switch directions and work to actively extend the toe more by pulling the toe away from the upright, holding a max RAILs contraction for 15 seconds.
Reset the toe in its deeper stretch position and hold the passive stretch for 30 seconds, and up to 2 minutes.
Repeat for 1-2 more reps on that toe before switching sides and repeating the process for the other toe.

name: Bilateral Shoulder Extension PRH Bent-Leg & Pike
cues: Grab a dowel with an overhand grip with the dowel positioned behind your body with your elbows straight.
Using either a bent-knee or straight-knee position, bend over and bring your shoulders into your passive end range of shoulder extension.
Take a breath in and create a full body contraction, working to actively extend your shoulders as much as you can.
Maintaining this contraction, slowly stand all the way up, aiming to actively keep your shoulders as close to your passive end range as possible.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing and bringing the dowel back to the body.
Reset the position and contraction, then perform the prescribed number of reps.

name: Bottoms Up Overhead Dual Kettlebell Carry
Bow & Arrow Complex
cues: Position 1 stick vertically directly to 1 side about 8-12 inches from the bod.

Grab the stick with both hands, with the bottom arm bent to 90 degrees holding the stick in the center and the top arm over the head grabbing the top of the stick while shifting the hips away from the direction of the stick.
While maintaining tension into the ground with the top hand, actively push the stick away with the bottom hand while laterally flexing the spine and driving the hips away.
Relax the tension into the stick while you stand straight back up to the start position.
Reset your tension, laterally flex the spine, and press the stick away again, completing the prescribed reps in this fashion.
On your last rep, you will hold the bottom position and perform rotations driven by the shoulder.
Keep the base of the stick in the ground and rotate the stick slightly in front of the body, then slightly behind the body.
Complete the prescribed number of rotations before switching the stick to the other side and repeating this process on the other side.

name: Breathing Anatomy
cues:
Breathing:   
Our primary breathing muscle is the diaphragm.
It is a large muscle that goes 360 degrees around the lowest portion of our ribs.
As the diaphragm contracts, it allows air in for inhalation, and as it relaxes, it pushes air out for exhalation.
We also use some secondary or accessory muscles for breathing, including the intercostal muscles between the ribs and the scalene muscles that connect the upper ribs to the neck.
These are not supposed to be used primarily for breathing but are often overused in people with increased pain, stress, or anxiety and can lead to neck and mid back pain.
The diaphragm is the top portion of our core.
It works in conjunction with the transverse abdominus and the pelvic floor muscles to create the foundation of our core.
We need to have a stable core to play sports, swing a golf club, or even lift weights.
If you think of shooting a canon from a rowboat vs, a stable surface, the canon will not shoot as far from the rowboat because it does not have a stable foundation.
This is why we need to be using our diaphragm for breathing, and we need to be able to use it independently and in conjunction without core muscles.

name: Butt kickers
cues: Focus on upright posture with a full range of motion for the knee.
Do not lean forward.

name: Butterfly PRH
cues: Position yourself in a butterfly base position, sitting tall, with the bottoms of your feet together.
Grasp your ankles or lower shins and relax while you use your elbows to press your legs to the floor, finding your passive end range of hip abduction.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to contract your hips as to pull your legs away from the support of your elbows.
Keeping the rest of the body still, slowly remove the support of the elbows and aim to maintain an active hip contraction as close to your passive end range as possible.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing and bringing your elbows back to meet your legs.
Find your passive end range again, reset your body tension, then complete this process for the designated number of reps holding a max contraction each time.

name: Butterfly PRLO
cues: Position yourself in a butterfly base position, sitting tall, with the bottoms of your feet together.
Grasp your ankles or lower shins and relax while you use your elbows to press your legs to the floor, finding your passive end range of hip abduction.
Then come out of this position 10-15 degrees, bringing the legs up slightly so that you have room to actively contract into.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to contract your hips and pull your legs away from the support of your elbows, finding your active end range.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing and bringing your legs back up to meet your elbows.
Reset your body tension, then complete this process for the designated number of reps holding a max contraction each time.

name: C Run Coaching
cues:
Exercise: “C” Run 
(aka: Butt-Kick Run with Mechanics, or Backside Recovery Drill) 
Purpose: 
The "C" Run develops the backside phase of the sprint cycle — focusing on hip extension, hamstring activation, and heel recovery.

It’s designed to: 
 
Improve stride efficiency 
Reinforce proper leg cycling 
Enhance glute and hamstring timing 
Reduce overstriding and promote a more fluid stride transition 
 
Unlike the A and B drills which emphasize frontside mechanics, the C Run shifts attention to what happens after toe-off — building efficient recovery and preparing the leg to cycle back under the hip.

Target Areas: 
 
Glute max (hip extension) 
Hamstrings (heel recovery, knee flexion) 
Calves (push-off and timing) 
Hip flexors (swing-leg repositioning) 
Core (trunk stability during movement) 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat, open space (10–20 meters) 
Athletic footwear or barefoot (on turf or safe surface) 
Ideally done after A and B run drills in a warm-up or sprint prep session 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Posture and Arms: 
 
 
Stay tall and upright, eyes forward 
Arms move front-to-back, elbows at ~90°, no cross-body swing 
Keep core engaged and spine neutral 
 
 
Leg Action: 
 
 
Perform a rhythmic running cycle where the heel is actively pulled up toward the glute after push-off 
Allow the knee to stay down — this is not a high-knee drill 
Emphasize quick heel recovery and tight, efficient backside motion 
The foot should sweep up and under, not flail behind you 
 
 
Ground Contact: 
 
 
Land on the ball of the foot, under the hip 
Keep ground contact quick and light 
 
 
Rhythm and Flow: 
 
 
Maintain consistent tempo and cadence — think "light, fast, efficient" 
The cycle should feel like it’s flowing, not forced 
 
Reps & Dosage: 
 
2–4 sets of 10–20 meters, walk back recovery 
Focus on quality movement and timing, not speed 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Pop the heel to the glute.” 
“Cycle tight, don’t swing long.” 
“Kick up and under, not behind.” 
“Stay tall and rhythmical.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Overextending the leg behind the body 
Opening the hips or trunk rotation 
Heel not lifting — dragging behind the stride 
Bouncing vertically instead of cycling efficiently 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Reinforces hamstring efficiency and timing — key to reducing hamstring injury risk 
Promotes a compact stride, minimizing overstriding or braking 
Complements A and B runs by completing the sprint cycle 
Helps transition from drill work into full sprinting with better leg mechanics 
 
When to Use: 
 
In sprint technique warm-ups or sprint development blocks 
During hamstring reconditioning or return-to-run protocols 
In coordination circuits for field and court sport athletes 
As part of a running mechanics reset 
 
Progressions: 
 
Combine with A- and B-runs for full-cycle sprint drill series 
Add light resistance bands to increase heel recovery activation 
Flow into acceleration sprints or build-ups 
Use a high-speed treadmill or curved sprint trainer for feedback.

name: C Skip Coaching
cues:
Exercise: C-Skip 
(aka: Heel-Recovery Skip, Backside Cycle Skip) 
Purpose: 
The C-Skip reinforces the recovery phase of the sprint stride by combining: 
 
Heel-to-glute recovery (backside) 
Knee lift and hip flexion (frontside) 
Foot repositioning under the center of mass 
Rhythm and timing of ground contact 
 
It helps athletes develop leg cycling mechanics — specifically how to recover the foot quickly and efficiently under the body, improving stride turnover, minimizing overstriding, and increasing running efficiency.

Target Areas: 
 
Hamstrings (heel recovery, knee flexion) 
Hip flexors (knee drive) 
Glutes and quads (postural support and coordination) 
Core (trunk control through movement) 
Ankle and foot (contact timing and rhythm) 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat surface (10–20 meters) 
Shoes or barefoot on turf/track 
Ideal to perform after A-Skip and B-Skip in a progression 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Posture and Arm Mechanics: 
 
 
Stand tall, ribs stacked over pelvis 
Arms bent ~90°, swing opposite to legs, front-to-back only (no crossover) 
 
 
Skip Cycle: 
 
 
Begin with a heel lift toward the glute, keeping the knee pointing down 
As the heel approaches the glute, transition into a knee drive, then snap the foot back down under the hips 
Land on the ball of the foot with a quick, reactive ground contact 
Repeat in a continuous, elastic skipping rhythm 
 
 
Rhythm and Timing: 
 
 
Focus on bounce + recover + strike 
The movement should feel cyclical and coordinated, not jerky or segmented 
 
Reps & Sets: 
 
2–3 sets of 10–20 meters 
Emphasize quality and cadence, not speed or power 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Heel to glute, knee up, foot down.” 
“Snap under the hips.” 
“Keep the rhythm tight.” 
“Stay tall, quick off the ground.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Overextending the leg backward (swinging instead of lifting) 
Knee lifting too soon before heel recovery 
Foot landing out in front (overstriding) 
Loss of rhythm or stiffness — flat foot contacts or excessive bounce 
Poor arm-leg coordination — arms not moving opposite to legs 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Reinforces efficient backside leg recovery and frontside transition 
Helps prevent overstriding and improves stride frequency 
Trains hamstring timing, a key factor in injury prevention 
Builds coordination and neuromuscular control of the full sprint cycle 
Prepares the athlete for top-speed sprinting and turnover drills 
 
When to Use: 
 
As part of a sprint warm-up or mechanics session 
In hamstring recovery or reconditioning 
During movement skill development in youth and field sport athletes 
As a rhythmic drill for improving gait timing and posture 
 
Progressions: 
 
C-Skip → C-Run (full stride recovery cycle) 
Add mini hurdles for spatial awareness 
Perform in-place for control, then move forward 
Combine with wall hip extension + recovery drills.

name: C Walk Coaching
cues:
Exercise: "C" Walk 
(aka: Butt Kick Walk with Sprint Mechanics or Backside Recovery Walk) 
Purpose: 
The C-Walk trains the backside phase of the sprint cycle, particularly: 
 
Hip extension mechanics 
Hamstring-controlled heel recovery 
Efficient stride turnover 
Postural control and rhythmic gait coordination 
 
It helps athletes build awareness of what happens after toe-off — the leg extending behind, then quickly and cleanly recovering under the hip for the next stride.

Target Areas: 
 
Hamstrings (knee flexion and foot recovery) 
Glutes (hip extension drive) 
Hip flexors (re-engaging for next cycle) 
Ankle and foot stabilizers (during heel lift and landing) 
Core/trunk stabilizers (to keep alignment) 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat, open space (10–15 yards) 
Athletic shoes or barefoot (on turf or track if barefoot) 
Performed after A-Walk and B-Walk for full cycle integration 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Posture and Start Position: 
 
 
Stand tall with arms bent at ~90° 
Core engaged, spine long, glutes lightly activated 
Begin walking forward with a controlled, rhythmic pace 
 
 
Heel Recovery Focus: 
 
 
As you walk, each leg extends behind the body (as in the end of a stride) 
Then the heel lifts up toward the glute, keeping the knee pointing down 
Avoid kicking the foot backward — instead, think heel up and under 
 
 
Stride Re-Cycling: 
 
 
After heel recovery, bring the leg back under the hip and step forward 
Keep foot strikes under your center of mass 
Arms move in opposition to the legs to reinforce sprint rhythm 
 
Reps & Dosage: 
 
2–3 sets of 10–15 yards 
Focus on smoothness, posture, and control — not speed 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Drive, extend, heel up, recover under.” 
“Foot to glute, knee down.” 
“Stay tall, cycle tight.” 
“Step underneath your hips.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Flinging the foot behind (not controlled recovery) 
Knee lifting with heel (turning it into a high knee or skip) 
Arched low back — loss of trunk posture 
Overstriding or slow cadence 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Reinforces the often-neglected backside mechanics of sprinting 
Improves hamstring timing and control, which is crucial for injury prevention 
Builds coordination between hip extension and foot recovery 
Sets up proper sequencing for B-Runs, C-Runs, and sprinting.

name: Cable Tricep Pushdown with Straight Bar
Chest Stretch Isometric (superband)
cues: Attach a thick band to post or doorway and put a hand through the loop and then grab both sides of the band.
Rotate away from the origin of the band.
Contract the chest structures that are stretching when you feel chest.
Hold the contraction for up to 30 seconds.

Rotate back to starting position.  
 
 
 
Repeat 1-2 times.  
 
 
 
Repeat on opposite side. 
 
 
this can be done against the wall or post without using the superband.
Place hand on doorway, post or wall.
Rotate away from your hand until you feel a good stretch.
Contract (PAILs) for up to 30 seconds.

You can follow with a RAILs contraction, or do multiple PAILs isometrics. 
 
 
See if you can rotate further after each contraction.

name: Collapsed Kneeling Plantar Flexion PAILs and RAILs
cues: Seated in a collapsed kneeling position, sit on your heels with the tops of your feet flat on the floor.
Passive Stretch - achieve a passive stretch of ankle plantar flexion by sitting all the way back on the heels and slowly relaxing for 2+ minutes.

PAILs - take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to rotate the feet and ankles into the floor, building up to a 100% contraction over the first 10 seconds, then holding the 100% contraction for another 10 seconds.
RAILs - quickly switch directions and work to pull the feet off of the floor, pulling the ankles into a greater plantar flexion stretch at 100% for 15 seconds.
Relax into the plantar flexion stretch for 30 seconds up to 2 minutes, and repeat this process again for 1-2 more reps.

name: Collapsed Kneeling Wrist Extension PRH
cues: From a combat base or kneeling position, place the palm of the hand on the floor outside the knees so that the fingers are facing forwards.
You can train each wrist individually or both at the same time.
Focus on your breathing while you slowly shift forwards to increase the wrist extension stretch.
Take a breath in and create full body tension then begin working to create more wrist extension by lifting the palm(s) off of the floor.
Maintaining this contraction, slowly shift the body back until you can clear the floor with your palm(s).
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing and shifting your body forwards and placing your palm(s) back to the floor.
Relax deeper into the stretch of wrist extension, reset your tension, then complete the designated number of reps.
Relax, switch arms, and repeat this process on the other side (if done individually).

name: Collapsed Kneeling Wrist Extension PRLO
cues: From a combat base or kneeling position, place the palm of the hand on the floor outside the knees so that the fingers are facing forwards.
You can train each wrist individually or both at the same time.
Focus on your breathing while you slowly shift forwards to increase the wrist extension stretch, finding your passive end range.
Shift your body back slightly to give your wrists space to actively contract into.
Take a breath in and create full body tension then begin working to create more wrist extension by lifting the palm(s) off of the floor.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing and placing your palm(s) back to the floor.
Reset your tension, then complete the designated number of reps.
Relax, switch arms, and repeat this process on the other side (if done individually).

name: Collapsed Quadruped Hip Extension ERR
cues: Position yourself in a collapsed quadruped position with your target leg straight.

Depending on your mobility, you may have your arms straight, elbows on the floor possibly with a foam roller or towel between your bent upper and lower leg, or in a fully collapsed quadruped position with your support leg bent and plantarflexed ankle on the floor - the lower you are to the ground, the more challenging it will be.
Take a breath in and create a full-body contraction, without moving any other part of the body, work to lift your straight leg as high into the air as possible.
Make sure you are targeting the glute/hamstring of the target leg, and are not getting more range of motion by extending the lumbar spine.
Hold for the designated period of time, then slowly lower the leg back down to the floor.
Reset your body tension, then complete for the designated number of reps.
Switch sides and repeat this process on the other leg.

name: Crocodile Breathing
cues: Begin face down, so that your stomach is on the floor.
Place your forehead on your hands, both palms down, one covering the other.
Make sure the chest and arms are relaxed, and you are as "flat" as you can get; your neck should be relaxed and comfortable.
You should feel that you are on your chest not on the edge of your ribs.
Action: Breathe in through the nose and feel the air move down past the chest into the "stomach".
When this happens, you will feel the abdomen push out against the ground, this should happen naturally without you forcing your stomach out.
You should feel the air “hit” the lower back first avoiding the upper back until the end of the inhale.
Take a nasal inhalation and exhalation.
Nasal inhalation should be a low, slow 3 seconds Then a brief pause Nasal exhalation should be slow and full 4-6 seconds Then a longer pause (2-3 seconds) Then the next breath cycle.
The air should expand in a 360-degree fashion filling the “cylinder” of the abdomen.

name: Crossover Step with Side Bend
cues: Stand tall with one stick placed vertically out to the side, driving down into the floor with the hand on the same side.
Take the leg closest to the stick and step across the body.
Laterally shift the hips away from the stick while laterally flexing the spine and reaching up and over towards the stick with the opposite side arm.
Step back across to the start position then repeat this process for 5-6 total reps.
Switch the stick to the other side of the body, now stepping across with the other leg, and repeat this process for 5-6 total reps going the other direction.

name: D Run or Butt Kickers Coaching
cues:
Purpose: 
 Butt Kickers are a foundational sprint drill used to develop hamstring activation, reinforce heel recovery mechanics, and build coordination and rhythm for running.
This drill helps athletes learn how to cycle the legs efficiently, training the rear-side mechanics of the sprint cycle — specifically how the heel travels toward the glute after toe-off.

Starting Position: 
 
Stand tall with posture upright — ears over shoulders, shoulders over hips, hips over ankles.
Arms bent at ~90 degrees and ready to swing in opposition to the legs.
Begin in place or at a slow jog moving forward.

Movement Pattern: 
 
Heel Recovery: 
 
 
Quickly lift one heel up toward the glute in a controlled, snapping motion.
The knee stays pointed down — this is not a high-knee drill.
Alternate legs rhythmically with a light bounce.

Posture and Arm Action: 
 
 
Maintain a tall, athletic posture with the spine straight and core engaged.
Arms swing in natural sprint rhythm, opposite the moving leg.

name: D Skip
cues:
Exercise: D-Skip (Butt Kicker Skip) 
(aka: Butt Kick Skip, Hamstring Recovery Skip, or Cyclic Heel Recovery Skip) 
Purpose: 
To develop the backside phase of the sprint cycle by coordinating: 
 
Hamstring-driven heel recovery 
Knee-down, foot-up mechanics 
Elastic rhythm and trunk control 
Timing and sequencing between arm swing and leg recovery 
 
D-Skips are ideal for reinforcing heel recovery mechanics that support efficient stride turnover and minimize overstriding — a key component in injury prevention and performance.

Target Areas: 
 
Hamstrings (active knee flexion) 
Glute max (postural control, propulsion support) 
Hip flexors (timing in frontside re-loading) 
Core stabilizers 
Ankle and foot stiffness (if done barefoot or on balls of feet) 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat surface (10–20 yards) 
Athletic shoes or barefoot (on turf or track if barefoot) 
Should follow D-Walk or C-Walk in a progression 
Can be done in place or moving forward 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Posture First: 
 
 
Stand tall, ribs stacked over pelvis 
Arms bent ~90°, ready to swing opposite to the legs 
Core lightly braced 
 
 
Skip and Recover: 
 
 
Perform a rhythmic skipping motion while pulling the heel toward the glute on each step 
The knee stays low and points downward — avoid turning this into a high-knee skip 
Stay on the balls of the feet, with quick and light ground contact 
The arms move naturally in opposition — like sprint mechanics 
 
 
Cadence and Rhythm: 
 
 
Keep the motion bouncy, elastic, and rhythmic 
Think heel up, reset under, not heel flinging back 
 
Reps & Sets: 
 
2–4 sets of 10–20 yards 
Quality over quantity — prioritize timing and coordination 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Heel to glute, knee down.” 
“Pop up and reset fast.” 
“Rhythm over height.” 
“Stay tall, land soft.” 
“Pull, don’t swing.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Heel flinging behind the body (lack of control) 
Knee lifting too high (becomes more like A-Skip) 
Excessive bounce — losing efficiency 
Toes pointing down — losing dorsiflexion and foot control 
Rotating the torso or arms across the body 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Recruits hamstring activity in sprint-like patterns 
Reinforces recovery cycle mechanics 
Teaches the short, tight, and fast foot turnover required in efficient sprinting 
Prepares the body for more dynamic drills, like C-Runs or bounding 
Especially valuable in return-to-sprint protocols or hamstring re-education 
 
When to Use: 
 
In the middle or end of a sprint prep sequence 
During running form development 
As part of a return-to-play program for hamstring rehab 
Integrated into track and field, field sport, or general athletic warm-ups 
 
Progressions: 
 
Transition to C-Runs (full stride mechanics) 
Combine with wall hip extension drills 
Add resistance bands for increased hamstring engagement 
Pair with dribble skips for stride frequency.

name: D Skip Coaching
cues:
Exercise: Butt Kicker Skip 
(aka: D-Skip, Hamstring Recovery Skip, or Heel-to-Glute Skip) 
Purpose: 
This drill emphasizes the heel recovery phase of the sprint stride — where the foot travels up toward the glute after push-off — and trains athletes to: 
 
Use the hamstrings to actively recover the leg 
Maintain proper posture and rhythm 
Improve stride timing and backside control 
 
It’s especially useful for sprinters, field athletes, and in return-to-run or hamstring rehab protocols.

Target Areas: 
 
Hamstrings (active heel recovery via knee flexion) 
Glutes and hip stabilizers (postural alignment) 
Hip flexors (stride reloading) 
Core (trunk stability and coordination) 
Foot and ankle (ground contact timing) 
 
Setup: 
 
10–20 meters of flat space 
Performed after A- and B-skips as a stride mechanics progression 
Shoes or barefoot (on turf/track if barefoot) 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Start in Tall Posture: 
 
 
Ribs stacked over pelvis 
Arms bent at ~90°, moving opposite to the legs 
Core braced gently 
 
 
Skip with Heel Recovery: 
 
 
Begin a skipping rhythm 
With each stride, actively pull your heel up toward your glute using the hamstring 
The knee stays down — don’t lift it like a high-knee skip 
The foot should cycle up and under, not swing behind 
 
 
Ground Contact: 
 
 
Land on the ball of the foot, directly under the hip 
Contacts should be quick, soft, and springy 
 
 
Coordination & Rhythm: 
 
 
Keep the movement tight and elastic — avoid exaggerated bounce 
Maintain a consistent arm-leg rhythm for efficient gait simulation 
 
Reps & Sets: 
 
2–3 sets of 10–20 meters 
Use as a precision drill — form and timing > speed 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Heel to glute, knee down.” 
“Snap the foot up, don’t fling it back.” 
“Quick, soft contact under the hip.” 
“Bounce and rhythm, not height.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Swinging the foot backward instead of lifting it up 
Lifting the knee (turns it into an A-skip) 
Toes pointing down — indicates poor dorsiflexion 
Landing in front of the body — causes overstriding and braking 
Vertical bounce — movement should be horizontal and fluid 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Trains hamstring coordination in sprint-like movement 
Reinforces the leg recovery path critical for efficient sprinting 
Helps prevent overstriding and hamstring strain by teaching tight, cyclical mechanics 
Improves timing and reactivity of ground contact 
Teaches athletes how to cycle the foot under the hips, not behind the body 
 
When to Use: 
 
In sprint warm-ups or technical prep 
As part of a hamstring reconditioning program 
Within a gait retraining sequence 
In movement skill development for multi-directional sport athletes 
 
Progressions: 
 
Butt Kicker Skip → C-Skip → C-Run 
Add mini hurdles or cones to cue step rhythm 
Perform in place first, then progress to forward movement 
Combine with wall hip extension + heel recovery drills.

name: D Walk
cues:
Exercise: D-Walk (Butt Kickers Walking) 
(aka: Butt Kicks Walk, Heel to Glute March, or Hamstring Recovery Walk) 
Purpose: 
The D-Walk reinforces the backside recovery phase of the running stride by teaching the athlete to: 
 
Lift the heel toward the glute using the hamstrings 
Maintain postural control during the movement 
Improve stride mechanics through hamstring awareness 
Develop coordination and timing for efficient sprinting 
 
It’s typically included in sprint drills to help athletes understand how to recover the leg properly after push-off, instead of overstriding or letting the leg trail inefficiently.

Target Areas: 
 
Hamstrings (concentric knee flexion) 
Glutes (postural support) 
Hip flexors (rhythmic recovery) 
Calves and ankle complex (if done with forefoot control) 
Core/trunk (to maintain upright posture) 
 
Setup: 
 
Flat surface, 10–15 yards 
Comfortable shoes or barefoot (on turf or safe surface) 
Ideal in warm-ups, sprint development, or movement re-education 
 
Movement Pattern: 
 
Posture First: 
 
 
Stand tall, spine neutral, ribs stacked over pelvis 
Arms bent ~90°, moving naturally with the gait cycle 
 
 
Step and Recover: 
 
 
Step forward and, as your foot leaves the ground, lift your heel toward your glute using the hamstrings 
The knee stays pointed down — this isn’t a high-knee drill 
Keep your toe dorsiflexed (pulled up), not floppy or pointing down 
 
 
Alternate Legs: 
 
 
Switch sides smoothly with a walking cadence 
Maintain an even rhythm and upright posture the entire time 
 
Reps & Sets: 
 
2–3 sets of 10–15 yards 
Can be done slowly for motor control, or slightly faster for rhythm 
 
Key Coaching Cues: 
 
“Heel to glute, knee stays down.” 
“Pull your foot up — don’t swing it back.” 
“Stay tall, soft landing.” 
“Toes up, not floppy.” 
 
Common Errors to Watch For: 
 
Swinging the foot backward instead of lifting it vertically 
Letting the knee lift (turning it into a skip) 
Overextending the low back — ribs flaring, pelvis tilting 
Toes pointing down — losing ankle control and weakening foot strike mechanics 
Bouncing vertically — movement should be smooth and low to the ground 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Trains the backside mechanics of running that are often neglected 
Reinforces hamstring coordination and recovery timing 
Prepares athletes for drills like C-Runs, bounding, and full-speed sprints 
Great for return-to-sport rehab, especially for hamstring or hip injuries 
 
When to Use: 
 
As part of a sprint mechanics warm-up 
In a running form re-education program 
Within a hamstring rehab protocol 
Paired with A/B/C drills for a complete sprint stride breakdown 
 
Progressions: 
 
Butt kicker skips 
C-Walk and C-Run 
Add band resistance around the ankles or thighs 
Pair with wall hip extension drills or eccentric hamstring strength work.

cues: Begin standing perpendicular to door with flexvit attached at elbow level.
Grasp band in outside arm and bend elbow to 90 degrees wrist in neutral position.

Externally rotate shoulder and bring tension into band.

Repeat for prescribed amount of sets and reps.

name: Dynamic Single-Leg Slapshot
cues: Stand with the feet together and a stick horizontal across the front of the body with a mixed grip.
One hand will hold the grip with an overhand grip, while the other hand holds the middle of the stick with an underhand grip.
You will then perform an RDL, standing on the leg that is on the same side as the hand that is holding the grip.
When you get to the bottom of the RDL, hold this position and drive the opposite end of the stick into the ground, bowing the stick.
Hold this tension for 5 seconds, then let the stick snap back as you drive up, forcing you to stabilize the forces.
As you come up, drive the free leg up into 90 degrees of hip and knee flexion while pulling the stick to your side.
Hold at the top for 1 second before dropping right into your next rep.
Complete the prescribed number of reps on the first leg, before switching sides and repeating this process on the other side of the body.

name: dynamic stick dead bug
cues: Lie on your back with your back flat to the floor and both legs straight.
Flex one hip to 90 degrees with the knee also bent to 90 degrees and both ankles flexed.
Holding the stick in the hand on the opposite side of the bent knee, drive the base of the stick into the top of the bent knee.
Simultaneously extend the free arm overhead and free leg straight out while maintaining your lower back flat on the floor throughout the set.
Bring the opposite arm/leg back to the start position, then repeat for the designated number of reps before switching sides.
You can increase the challenge by placing your hand higher up on the stick.
Only go as far as you can while maintaining a flat lower back.

name: Elbow Flexion PRH
cues: In a kneeling, seated, or standing position, position your working arm at your end range of elbow flexion, using your support arm to press the forearm against the upper arm.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to create as much active elbow flexion as possible, squeezing the biceps hard.
Slowly remove the support arm and work to maintain active elbow flexion as close to your passive end range as possible.
Hold for the designated period of time.
Relax, then bring your support arm back to the working arm, and find your passive end range again.
Reset your tension then complete the designated number of reps.
Relax, switch arms, then repeat this process on other other side.

name: Elbow Flexion PRLO
cues: In a kneeling, seated, or standing position, position your working arm at your end range of elbow flexion, using your support arm to press the forearm against the upper arm.
Then come out of this end range slightly so that you have space to actively contract into.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to create as much active elbow flexion as possible, pulling the working arm away from the support arm.
Hold for the designated period of time.
Relax, then bring your working arm back to the support arm.
Reset your tension then complete the designated number of reps.
Relax, switch arms, then repeat this process on other other side.

name: Elbow Pronation PRH
cues: In a kneeling, seated, or standing position, position your working arm bent to 90 degrees with the palm down and inside elbow touching the side of the body.
Grasp the lower forearm with the control hand, working to rotate the forearm internally into its passive end range of elbow pronation.
Focus on your breathing while you use the control hand to guide the elbow deeper into internal rotation (pronation).
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then begin to maximally pronate the elbow into your active end range.
Remove the control hand and work to maintain active pronation as close to your passive end range as possible.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing your tension and bringing your control hand back to the working arm.
Use the control hand to guide the elbow deeper into pronation, reset your tension, then complete the designated number of reps.
Relax, switch arms, and repeat this process on the other side.

name: Elbow Pronation PRLO
cues: In a kneeling, seated, or standing position, position your working arm bent to 90 degrees with the palm down and inside elbow touching the side of the body.
Grasp the lower forearm with the control hand, working to rotate the forearm internally into its passive end range of elbow pronation.
Then come out of the end range slightly so that you have room to actively rotate into.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to internally rotate (pronate) the elbow at maximum effort.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing and bringing the arm back to the control hand.
Reset your tension then complete the designated number of reps.
Relax, switch arms, then repeat this process on the other side.

name: Elbow Supination PRH
cues: In a kneeling, seated, or standing position, position your working arm bent to 90 degrees with the palm up and inside elbow touching the side of the body.
Grasp the lower forearm with the control hand, working to rotate the forearm externally into its passive end range of elbow pronation.
Focus on your breathing while you use the control hand to guide the elbow deeper into external rotation (supination).
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then begin to maximally supinate the elbow into your active end range.
Remove the control hand and work to maintain active supination as close to your passive end range as possible.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing your tension and bringing your control hand back to the working arm.
Use the control hand to guide the elbow deeper into supination, reset your tension, then complete the designated number of reps.
Relax, switch arms, and repeat this process on the other side.

name: Elbow Supination PRLO (1)
cues: In a kneeling, seated, or standing position, position your working arm bent to 90 degrees with the palm up and inside elbow touching the side of the body.
Grasp the lower forearm with the control hand, working to rotate the forearm externally into its passive end range of elbow supination.
Then come out of the end range slightly so that you have room to actively rotate into.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to externally rotate (supinate) the elbow at maximum effort, pulling away from the control hand.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing and bringing the arm back to the control hand.
Reset your tension then complete the designated number of reps.
Relax, switch arms, then repeat this process on the other side.

name: Elevated Pigeon with Forward Flexion
cues: With the sticks out in front, driving vertically down into the ground, position yourself in a pigeon stretch with one leg bent across the body positioned onto a box, chair, etc.
Keep the down leg straight with the foot facing forward.
While driving the sticks down, complete 5 reps moving the torso forward/down by hinging at the hips and staying long in the spine.
On the 5th rep, lock in the bottom position and drive the sticks into the ground hard for 5 seconds.
Press yourself up back to the start position and rotate your torso in the direction of the elevated foot.
Complete another 5 reps moving the torso forward with rotation, again hinging at the hips and staying long in the spine.
On your 5th rep, you will hold the bottom position and drive the sticks hard into the ground for 5 seconds.
Push yourself back up to the start position and rotate to the other side and complete 5 more reps with a 5 second hold at the bottom of the 5th rep.
Find areas that you do not move as well and spend more time in those positions.
Then switch legs and repeat this process on the other side.

name: Figure 4 Hip Flexion PRH
cues: Position yourself in a Figure 4 base position with your target leg straight and chest tall.
Place your hands on either side of the target leg with the elbows bent.
Find your passive end range of hip flexion by shifting your hips back and chest forward.
Take a breath in and create a full body contraction, driving tension into the target leg as you try to pull the leg off of the floor.
Hold that max contraction as you drive your hands into the floor and extend the elbows, pushing your body back, lifting the leg off of the floor.
Hold for the designated period of time then slowly lower your leg back to the floor.
Perform for the designated sets and reps before repeating the process on the other leg.

name: Finger Extension ERR
cues: Set your palm completely flat on a surface with your fingers spread.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to actively lift the first finger as high into extension as you can.
Maintaining this tension, begin to draw either small or large clockwise circles with the working finger.
Complete the designated number of reps before switching directions and drawing counter-clockwise circles, always working to extend the finger as high into your active end range as possible.
Complete the designated number of reps before bringing the finger back down to the flat surface.
After the first finger is complete, follow the same process for all of the other fingers before switching sides.

name: Finger Extension Hover
cues: Set your palm completely flat on a surface with your fingers spread.
Position an object like an eraser or any other small object to the inside of the first finger.
The objects height should be slightly less than your active end range of extension.
Take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to actively lift the finger up into extension, hover over the object, then slowly set it down on the other side.
Reset your tension, then bring the finger back up and over the object, returning the finger to its starting position.
Reset your tension, then complete the designated number of reps.
After the first finger is complete, follow the same process for all of the other fingers before switching sides.

name: Finger Extension PRH
cues: Set your palm completely flat on a surface with your fingers spread.

Take a breath in and create full body tension, then slowly let go of the finger and working to maintain active extension as close to your passive end range as possible.
Hold for the prescribed amount of time, then grab the finger again, bringing it back into its passive range.
Complete the designated number of reps, always working to maximize active extension without compensation in the rest of the hand.
After the first finger is complete, follow the same process for all of the other fingers before switching sides.

name: Finger Extension PRLO

Take a breath in and create full body tension, then work to actively lift the finger off of the object.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing and bringing the finger back down to the object.
Reset your tension, then complete the designated number of reps.

name: Heel raises with big toe resistance
cues:
Purpose: 
To strengthen the calves and improve foot-ankle stability, while emphasizing pressure through the big toe to enhance arch control and medial foot activation.
This variation trains proper foot mechanics and helps reinforce the kinetic chain from the ground up.

Instructions: 
 
Set Up: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, barefoot or in minimalist shoes.
Before you begin, focus on actively pressing your big toe into the ground — this will anchor your medial foot and prevent collapse of the arch.
Engage: Slightly grip the floor with the big toe and ball of the foot.
Imagine "spreading" the foot wide and creating a tripod base — big toe, pinky toe, and heel all grounded.
Movement: Slowly rise up onto the balls of your feet while keeping that big toe pressure active.
Hold briefly at the top, then lower under control.
Avoid letting your weight shift to the outer edge of the foot — stay centered through the big toe.

name: Knee CAR How To
cues:
Purpose: 
To assess and improve control of the knee joint, especially its ability to move through flexion, extension, and rotation. Though it's primarily a hinge joint, the knee also has active internal and external rotation — particularly when the knee is bent. 
Knee CARs help improve: 
 
Joint capsule health 
Muscle activation around the knee 
Proprioception and neuromuscular control 
Post-rehab reintegration 
Injury prevention in cutting, sprinting, and squatting sports 
 
Target Areas: 
 
Quadriceps (knee extension) 
Hamstrings (knee flexion) 
Popliteus and rotator muscles (internal/external rotation) 
Joint capsule and synovial health 
 
Setup: 
 
Sit on the floor or bench with the hip at 90° flexion, thigh supported. 
You can use your hands to hold under the thigh to prevent it from moving. 
Make sure the hip stays still — movement should come from the knee down only. 
 
Movement Pattern:.

Start in Full Knee Flexion: 
 
Bend the knee fully so your heel is close to your hamstring.

Lock in External Rotation: 
 
Rotate the shin outward (external tibial rotation) — think of your foot turning outward, like pointing your toes away from your midline. 
Hold this rotation.

Extend the Knee: 
 
While maintaining external rotation, straighten the leg slowly all the way to full extension.

Rotate Internally at the Top: 
 
At full extension, rotate the foot inward (internal tibial rotation). 
You’ll feel different muscles activating — this is the tibia rotating inside the knee joint.

Flex the Knee Back Down: 
 
While holding internal rotation, bend the knee back to the start position.

Return to External Rotation at the Bottom: 
 
You’ve completed one controlled circle — now reverse the direction and repeat. 
 
Reps & Frequency: 
 
2–3 reps per direction, per leg 
Daily for joint health, or before training/rehab sessions 
 
Key Coaching Points: 
 
Control is everything — go slowly (5–10 seconds per rep). 
Don’t let your hip or thigh rotate — isolate the knee. 
Maintain consistent tension throughout the range — no swinging or slacking. 
You may feel “crunchiness” — that’s often normal unless it's painful. 
 
Why It’s Important: 
 
Knee rotation is critical for functional movement — especially in sports with cutting, pivoting, or deep knee angles. 
Enhances joint capsule integrity, reduces stiffness, and improves brain-body connection. 
Ideal for post-ACL or meniscus surgery to restore full joint control. 
Helps prevent overload in neighboring joints (hip/ankle) from knee immobility. 
 
When to Use: 
 
Daily mobility routine 
Pre-training warm-up (especially lower body days) 
During or after knee rehab 
Movement screening for athletes or clients with knee history 
 
Progressions: 
 
Add light ankle weights or resistance for end-range strength 
Incorporate isometric holds at key angles 
Do in closed chain (standing with knee bent) for more functional loading 
 
Complementary Drills: 
 
Seated knee extension isometrics 
TKEs (terminal knee extensions) for quad control 
Step-downs or Poliquin step-ups for functional knee control 
Hip and ankle CARs to support the full chain.

name: Kneeling Hip Extension Eccentric Neural Grooving
cues: Position yourself in a 1/2 kneeling base position holding onto a wall, sticks, or any stable object.
Posteriorly tilt your pelvis by tucking your tailbone under your body and squeezing the glute of the knee that is on the ground.
Take a breath in and create a full body contraction, then without moving the knee, create a contraction as if to pull the grounded knee forward and up into hip flexion.
Maintaining this contraction and tension, slowly begin shifting your body forward, creating a stretch on the anterior hip tissues while they contract.
Shift forward until you can no longer maintain the contraction, relax your tension, then use your hands and/or front foot to press you back to your starting position.
Reset your tension and contraction, then complete the designated number of reps before switching sides.
The amount of reps, the time for each rep, and the amount of tension you create will be variables dependent on your program.

Focus on your breathing while you slowly inch your hand up the stick, taking the shoulder deeper into external rotation, finding your passive end range.

Take a deep breath in and create full body tension squeezing the ball tight, and loosen the grip on the stick, working to maintain active external rotation as close to your passive end range as possible.
Hold for the designated period of time before relaxing and resetting your grip on the stick.
Reset your body tension then complete the designated number of reps.
Relax, switch arms, then repeat this process on the other side.
